Issued at 320 PM CDT Mon Aug 17 2026

Mid and upper-level flow is zonal across the Central CONUS today 
with a ridge axis over the Intermountain West. Surface anticyclone 
currently sits underneath it which has presented the mild weather 
conditions for Monday. There are several short-wave perturbations 
over the Rockies though that will result in dCVA over the Front 
Range and Lee Cyclogenesis, with pressure falls extending eastward 
into the Plains starting on Tuesday morning. Convection will likely 
be occurring over the Central Plains and attempt to move eastward 
toward the area. 

For the forecast area Tuesday, H5 height falls will slowly continue 
through much of the day as surface cyclone strengthens over the High 
Plains of Kansas. Surface pressure falls remain progged to expand 
eastward into the lower Missouri River Valley, which will provide an 
increase in convergence heading into the afternoon. The short-wave 
perturbations will also aid in providing deep layer shear, gradually 
increasing to 35 to 40 kts of 0-6km bulk shear by the afternoon. A 
cold front is expected to develop and be positioned on the backside 
of the developing cyclone. Surface winds throughout Tuesday 
afternoon will turn more southerly, and provide stronger theta-e 
transport, resulting in increasing dewpoint temperatures. Convection 
over the Plains, whether or not it develops and propagates 
downstream, is largely going to determine what will happen in the 
afternoon across eastern Kansas to Central Missouri. Current CAM 
guidance has the organized convective complex over Nebraska decaying 
before reaching northwest Missouri. However, this starts to send an 
outflow boundary southeastward into the forecast area, that could 
provide further initiation downstream. If activity is able to 
develop along this, there may be enough deep layer shear to help try 
and organize it. However, very uncertain how much CAPE will be there 
in the presence of any outflow boundary potential. From the 12z 
HREF, MUCAPE values prior to 18z Tuesday afternoon struggle to climb 
much above 750 J/kg. Cirrus clouds advecting from overnight 
convection in Nebraska may slow the rate destabilization into 
northeast Kansas and Central Missouri, which would limit the severe 
threat if anything develops after 12z Tuesday morning in the 
forecast area. As of right now, the expectation is that there will 
be scattered shower and storm activity, but with a limited severe 
threat is any at all. We will need to pay close attention to 
instability trends Tuesday morning and afternoon. If the boundary 
layer is able to rapidly destabilize, Tuesday afternoon shower 
activity could deepen and become more robust. 

Attention then turns to the Tuesday evening, and heading into the 
overnight hours. Surface pressure falls will continue as the surface 
cyclone propagates eastward toward the lower Missouri River Valley. 
Continued mid-level height falls will also provide more broadscale 
lift across much of the region, with southerly winds continuing to 
provide theta-e advection, which should help bump up CAPE values 
substantially. The timing still remains uncertain, and occurrence 
still conditional, as afternoon activity and remnant outflow 
boundary placement looks to largely be in control of the mesoscale 
environment. CAM guidance continues to depict the new development of 
storms in central and eastern Kansas between 23-01z in the evening, 
largely tied to the cold front and mid-level lift from the mid-level 
short-wave vort maxima. This will then move toward the southeast 
along the axis of increasing surface pressure falls. These storms 
are expected to have more instability to work with. However, what is 
uncertain is if storms will be surface based, or if they will become 
more elevated. Central Kansas and areas just west of the forecast 
area will have the best chances for isolated and discrete convection 
after peak heating. Unsure if discrete activity will continue into 
far eastern Kansas and western Missouri. If storms remain discrete 
and surface based after 00z as they move toward the east-southeast, 
backing surface winds and curved low-level hodographs can favor the 
development of supercells. There is enough SRH that could support a 
tornado threat, along with healthy mid-level CAPE through the hail 
growth zone allowing for larger hail stones, and the damaging wind 
gusts. Our western zones seem to favor the most potential for this 
threat if it is realized, while the potential for discrete 
convection and supercell storms east of Interstate 35 is greatly 
diminished. If the discrete convection remains well west of the 
area, the low-level jet is expected to congeal any storm activity 
over Central Kansas into an MCS. 0-3km bulk shear between 40-50 kts
